questions.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ on $[1,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $a=1,$ and $b=2.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}{x}\,\text{d}x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)$ on $[1,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x),$ $a=1,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡x
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{1+{(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}|\operatorname{csc}⁡x|\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note, that we use $|\operatorname{csc}⁡x|=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$, which is valid due to that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x>0$ on $[1,3].$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}{({x}^{2}+2)}^{3/2},$ $a=2,$ and $b=5.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{({x}^{2}+2)}^{1/2}\cdot 2x=x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+2)}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+2)}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}={x}^{2}+1$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}({x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x)|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}(5)^{3}+(5)]-[\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}+(2)] \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}},$ $a=0,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}(2-{x}^{2})^{-1/2}(-2x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2-{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}}{2-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}))|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})]-[\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}})] \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})-0 \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x,$ $a=-1,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}=\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{(1-x)^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+1-2x+{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2-2x}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2(1-x)}{(1-x)(1+x)}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1+x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+x}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+1}-2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+(-1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2})-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={x}^{1/2}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{1/2}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{2}{3}{(1+x)}^{3/2}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[{4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4x+4}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4x+4}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{4x+4}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \sqrt{x+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\sqrt{x+1}+1.$

L={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}.

canonical_examples.problem: What is the arc length of the curve $y = \arccos{x}$ on $\left[0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)= \arccos{x} ,$ $a=0,$ and $b=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) =-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
$$

Substituting $f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac{2-{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Compute the arc length of  the curve $y=x^{3/2}$ between the points $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{4}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010575/assets/4ed8b94a4fff3c22697264e467f955f2e51a62618d03295c4e4f38493bff2ced.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)= x^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=\dfrac{4}{3}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) =   \dfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt { 1 + [f'(x)]^2 }\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{9}{4}x} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+9x}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(4+9x)} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}\sqrt{4+9x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4+9x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt { 1 + [f'(x)]^2 } = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{4 + 9x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{4}{3}}\sqrt{4+9x}\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u= 4+9x.$ Then, $\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{9}\textrm{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{4}{3} \\ u & 4 & 16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{4}{3}}\sqrt{4+9x}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{4}^{16}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{9}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{\int }_{4}^{16}{u}^{\frac{1}{2}}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{\frac{3}{2}}]}_{4}^{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{\frac{3}{2}}]}_{4}^{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{27}([(16)^{\frac{3}{2}}]-[(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}([64]-[8]) \\  & =\frac{56}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\displaystyle  \int_{5}^{6} } \sqrt{1+\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}}  \,\textrm{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve? 

- $y=  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-16}}$

- $y=  \sqrt{x^2-16} + \sqrt 5$

- $y=  \dfrac{x}{x^2-16} + 1$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L=\int_{5}^{6}  \sqrt{1+\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}}  \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[f'(x)]^2=\dfrac {x^2}{x^2-16}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(x) = \pm \dfrac {x}{\sqrt{x^2-16}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=  \sqrt{x^2-16} + \sqrt 5.$
